title: Chapter I

teacherSummary.text: The novel opens with its famous ironic line about a single man in possession of a good fortune. Mrs. Bennet excitedly tells Mr. Bennet that a wealthy young man, Mr. Bingley, has rented Netherfield Park; Mr. Bennet teases her.

context.history: In Regency England, daughters of gentry families depended on marriage for security; the Bennet estate is entailed away from daughters.

significance: The opening sentence is among the most quoted in English and models Austen's irony: it means the reverse of what it seems to say.
discussionQuestions: What does the first sentence really suggest about who wants the marriage?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter I,” how does Austen show marriage as a social goal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter I develops the idea of marriage as a social goal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter I to complicate the reader's understanding of marriage as a social goal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter I within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of marriage as a social goal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter I as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of marriage as a social goal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: What does the first sentence really suggest about who wants the marriage? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include newcomers, develop, caprice, tiresome, recommend. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general you know they visit no newcomers.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: One who has lately come.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. In Regency England, daughters of gentry families depended on marriage for security; the Bennet estate is entailed away from daughters. Now, why does this chapter matter? The opening sentence is among the most quoted in English and models Austen's irony: it means the reverse of what it seems to say. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot irony, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: “My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”

segments.script: Now it is your turn. First, the chapter quiz in the app. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter I,” how does Austen show marriage as a social goal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference with you.

segments.activity: One-sentence claim plus one quoted piece of evidence.
segments.script: To close: in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about marriage as a social goal, and back it with one short quotation. Hand it to me on your way out.
